    A_v f = p f(.,v=1) + q f(.,v=0)  -- carrying the frequencies omitting v --
    and the v-derivative D_v f = f(.,v=1) - f(.,v=0) -- whose coefficients are,
    by the identity fhat(S) = (D_v f)^(S \\ v), exactly the coefficients of f at
    the frequencies containing v.  The normalising powers (pq)^{|S|} cancel
    automatically, so no division ever occurs.
    """
    q = 1 - p
    F: List[Rat] = list(f)
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for eta in range(1 << n):
            if eta & bit:
                continue
            a = F[eta]           # site v closed
            b = F[eta | bit]     # site v open
            F[eta] = p * b + q * a
            F[eta | bit] = b - a
    return F


def level_energies(p: Rat, n: int, fhat: Sequence[Rat]) -> List[Rat]:
    """E_S(f) = (pq)^{|S|} fhat(S)^2 for every frequency S."""
    pq = p * (1 - p)
    return [pq ** popcount(s) * fhat[s] ** 2 for s in range(1 << n)]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Discrete calculus on the cube                                               #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def flip_to(eta: Config, v: int, open_: bool) -> Config:
    """The configuration eta with site v reset to open/closed."""
    return (eta | (1 << v)) if open_ else (eta & ~(1 << v))


def derivative(n: int, f: Sequence[Rat], v: int) -> List[Rat]:
    """D_v f (eta) = f(eta with v open) - f(eta with v closed)."""
    return [f[flip_to(eta, v, True)] - f[flip_to(eta, v, False)]
            for eta in all_configs(n)]


def variance(p: Rat, n: int, f: Sequence[Rat]) -> Rat:
    """Var_p(f) = E_p[f^2] - (E_p[f])^2."""
    sq = [x * x for x in f]
    m = expectation(p, n, f)
    return expectation(p, n, sq) - m * m


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Events                                                                      #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def sign_indicator(n: int, member: Callable[[Config], bool]) -> List[Rat]:
    """The +/-1 indicator g_A of the event A described by `member`."""
    return [Rat(1) if member(eta) else Rat(-1) for eta in all_configs(n)]


def probability(p: Rat, n: int, member: Callable[[Config], bool]) -> Rat:
    """P_p(A)."""
    return sum(weight(p, n, eta) for eta in all_configs(n) if member(eta))


def influence(p: Rat, n: int, member: Callable[[Config], bool], v: int) -> Rat:
    """
    I_v = P_p(site v is pivotal): the probability that opening v puts the
    configuration in A while closing it does not.
    """
    tot = Rat(0)
    for eta in all_configs(n):
        if member(flip_to(eta, v, True)) and not member(flip_to(eta, v, False)):
            tot += weight(p, n, eta)
    return tot


def is_increasing(n: int, member: Callable[[Config], bool]) -> bool:
    """Brute-force monotonicity check: opening a site never destroys the event."""
    for eta in all_configs(n):
        if not member(eta):
            continue
        for v in range(n):
            if not member(eta | (1 << v)):
                return False
    return True


# Concrete increasing events -------------------------------------------------

def dictator(v: int) -> Callable[[Config], bool]:
    return lambda eta: bool((eta >> v) & 1)


def majority(n: int) -> Callable[[Config], bool]:
    return lambda eta: 2 * popcount(eta) > n


def and_all(n: int) -> Callable[[Config], bool]:
    return lambda eta: popcount(eta) == n


def or_all(n: int) -> Callable[[Config], bool]:
    return lambda eta: eta != 0


def tribes(groups: Sequence[Sequence[int]]) -> Callable[[Config], bool]:
    """OR of ANDs: at least one group entirely open."""
    masks = [sum(1 << v for v in g) for g in groups]
    return lambda eta: any((eta & m) == m for m in masks)


def grid_row_crossing(n: int) -> Callable[[Config], bool]:
    """
    Horizontal crossing of the n x n grid in the simplest sense: some row is
    entirely open.  Site (i, j) is bit i*n + j.  This event is increasing.
    """
    masks = [sum(1 << (i * n + j) for j in range(n)) for i in range(n)]
    return lambda eta: any((eta & m) == m for m in masks)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Verification routines                                                       #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def check(label: str, lhs: Rat, rhs: Rat) -> None:
    status = "OK " if lhs == rhs else "FAIL"
    print(f"    [{status}] {label:<52} {str(lhs):>18} == {str(rhs):>18}")
    assert lhs == rhs, f"{label}: {lhs} != {rhs}"


def verify_orthogonality(p: Rat, n: int) -> None:
    """E_p[psi_S psi_T] = [S=T] (pq)^{|S|}."""
    pq = p * (1 - p)
    bad = 0
    for s in range(1 << n):
        for t in range(1 << n):
            val = sum(weight(p, n, eta) * psi_set(p, n, eta, s) * psi_set(p, n, eta, t)
                      for eta in all_configs(n))
            expect = pq ** popcount(s) if s == t else Rat(0)
            if val != expect:
                bad += 1
    print(f"    [{'OK ' if bad == 0 else 'FAIL'}] orthogonality over all "
          f"{(1 << n) ** 2} pairs of frequencies")
    assert bad == 0


def verify_completeness(p: Rat, n: int, f: Sequence[Rat]) -> None:
    """f(eta) = sum_S fhat(S) psi_S(eta)."""
    fhat = fourier_coefficients(p, n, f)
    for eta in all_configs(n):
        recon = sum(fhat[s] * psi_set(p, n, eta, s) for s in range(1 << n))
        assert recon == f[eta], f"reconstruction failed at {eta}"
    print(f"    [OK ] completeness: f = sum_S fhat(S) psi_S at all {1 << n} points")


def verify_parseval(p: Rat, n: int, f: Sequence[Rat], g: Sequence[Rat]) -> None:
    pq = p * (1 - p)
    fhat = fourier_coefficients(p, n, f)
    ghat = fourier_coefficients(p, n, g)
    lhs = expectation(p, n, [f[e] * g[e] for e in all_configs(n)])
    rhs = sum(pq ** popcount(s) * fhat[s] * ghat[s] for s in range(1 << n))
    check("Parseval  E[fg] = sum_S (pq)^|S| fhat ghat", lhs, rhs)


def verify_site_energy_and_efron_stein(p: Rat, n: int, f: Sequence[Rat]) -> None:
    """
    sum_{S ni v} E_S(f) = pq E[(D_v f)^2]   and the exact Efron-Stein defect.
    """
    pq = p * (1 - p)
    fhat = fourier_coefficients(p, n, f)
    en = level_energies(p, n, fhat)

    for v in range(n):
        lhs = sum(en[s] for s in range(1 << n) if (s >> v) & 1)
        d = derivative(n, f, v)
        rhs = pq * expectation(p, n, [x * x for x in d])
        check(f"site energy identity at site {v}", lhs, rhs)

    total_deriv = sum(expectation(p, n, [x * x for x in derivative(n, f, v)])
                      for v in range(n))
    defect_lhs = pq * total_deriv - variance(p, n, f)
    defect_rhs = sum((Rat(popcount(s)) - 1) * en[s]
                     for s in range(1 << n) if s != 0)
    check("Efron-Stein defect identity", defect_lhs, defect_rhs)
    assert defect_lhs >= 0, "Poincare inequality violated"
    print(f"    [OK ] Poincare inequality Var <= pq sum_v E[(D_v f)^2] "
          f"(slack {defect_lhs})")


def analyse_event(name: str, p: Rat, n: int,
                  member: Callable[[Config], bool]) -> Dict[str, Rat]:
    """Full spectral analysis of one increasing event, verifying every identity."""
    q = 1 - p
    pq = p * q
    print(f"\n  --- {name}   (N = {n} sites, p = {p}) ---")
    assert is_increasing(n, member), "event is not increasing"

    g = sign_indicator(n, member)
    ghat = fourier_coefficients(p, n, g)
    ghat_fast = fast_biased_transform(p, n, g)
    check("fast transform agrees with the definition",
          Rat(int(list(ghat) == list(ghat_fast))), Rat(1))

    en = level_energies(p, n, ghat)
    P = probability(p, n, member)
    infl = [influence(p, n, member, v) for v in range(n)]

    print(f"    P = {P},   influences = {[str(i) for i in infl]}")

    # 1. Plancherel for Boolean functions
    check("Plancherel   sum_S E_S = 1", sum(en), Rat(1))

    # 2. degree-0 and degree-1 coefficients
    check("ghat(empty) = 2P - 1", ghat[0], 2 * P - 1)
    for v in range(n):
        check(f"Margulis-Russo  ghat({{{v}}}) = 2 I_{v}", ghat[1 << v], 2 * infl[v])

    # 3. exact energy decomposition (the l^2 influence bound with its defect)
    high = sum(en[s] for s in range(1 << n) if popcount(s) >= 2)
    lhs = 4 * P * (1 - P)
    rhs = 4 * pq * sum(i * i for i in infl) + high
    check("energy decomposition 4P(1-P) = 4pq sum I_v^2 + R", lhs, rhs)
    l2_defect = high / 4
    assert pq * sum(i * i for i in infl) + l2_defect == P * (1 - P)
    print(f"    l^2 bound     pq sum I_v^2 = {pq * sum(i * i for i in infl)}"
          f"  <=  P(1-P) = {P * (1 - P)}   (defect {l2_defect})")

    # 4. exact Poincare defect
    poin_lhs = 4 * pq * sum(infl) - 4 * P * (1 - P)
    poin_rhs = sum((Rat(popcount(s)) - 1) * en[s] for s in range(1 << n) if s != 0)
    check("Poincare defect 4pq sum I_v - 4P(1-P)", poin_lhs, poin_rhs)
    print(f"    Poincare      P(1-P) = {P * (1 - P)}"
          f"  <=  pq sum I_v = {pq * sum(infl)}   (defect {poin_rhs / 4})")

    # 5. total influence in Fourier form
    check("4pq sum I_v = sum_S |S| E_S",
          4 * pq * sum(infl),
          sum(Rat(popcount(s)) * en[s] for s in range(1 << n)))

    # 6. the unified equality criterion
    degree_le_one = all(ghat[s] == 0 for s in range(1 << n) if popcount(s) >= 2)
    l2_tight = (pq * sum(i * i for i in infl) == P * (1 - P))
    poin_tight = (P * (1 - P) == pq * sum(infl))
    check("l^2 tight  <=>  degree <= 1",
          Rat(int(l2_tight)), Rat(int(degree_le_one)))
    check("Poincare tight  <=>  degree <= 1",
          Rat(int(poin_tight)), Rat(int(degree_le_one)))
    print(f"    degree <= 1 : {degree_le_one}   -> both inequalities "
          f"{'are equalities' if degree_le_one else 'are strict'}")

    # spectral profile by degree
    profile = {}
    for s in range(1 << n):
        profile[popcount(s)] = profile.get(popcount(s), Rat(0)) + en[s]
    print("    spectral profile by degree: "
          + ", ".join(f"{k}: {v}" for k, v in sorted(profile.items())))

    return {"P": P, "l2_defect": l2_defect, "poincare_defect": poin_rhs / 4}


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Main                                                                        #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("  THE COMPLETE p-BIASED FOURIER EXPANSION ON THE DISCRETE CUBE")
    print("  exact rational verification of every identity")
    print("=" * 78)

    # ---- Part 1: the basis itself ----------------------------------------- #
    print("\n[1] Orthogonality and completeness of the biased characters")
    for p in (Rat(1, 2), Rat(1, 3), Rat(2, 5)):
        print(f"\n  p = {p}")
        verify_orthogonality(p, 3)
        rng = random.Random(20260807)
        f = [Rat(rng.randint(-9, 9), rng.randint(1, 5)) for _ in range(1 << 3)]
        verify_completeness(p, 3, f)
        g = [Rat(rng.randint(-9, 9), rng.randint(1, 5)) for _ in range(1 << 3)]
        verify_parseval(p, 3, f, g)

    # ---- Part 2: Efron-Stein for arbitrary (non-Boolean) functions --------- #
    print("\n[2] The exact Efron-Stein / Poincare defect for arbitrary functions")
    rng = random.Random(11235)
    for p in (Rat(1, 2), Rat(1, 4)):
        print(f"\n  random rational function on 3 sites, p = {p}")
        f = [Rat(rng.randint(-6, 6), rng.randint(1, 4)) for _ in range(1 << 3)]
        verify_site_energy_and_efron_stein(p, 3, f)

    # ---- Part 3: increasing events ---------------------------------------- #
    print("\n[3] Increasing events: both influence inequalities and their defects")

    summary: List[Tuple[str, Rat, Rat]] = []

    r = analyse_event("Dictatorship on site 0", Rat(1, 3), 3, dictator(0))
    summary.append(("Dictatorship (p=1/3)", r["l2_defect"], r["poincare_defect"]))

    r = analyse_event("Majority of 3", Rat(1, 2), 3, majority(3))
    summary.append(("Majority-3 (p=1/2)", r["l2_defect"], r["poincare_defect"]))

    r = analyse_event("AND of 3", Rat(1, 2), 3, and_all(3))
    summary.append(("AND-3 (p=1/2)", r["l2_defect"], r["poincare_defect"]))

    r = analyse_event("OR of 3", Rat(1, 2), 3, or_all(3))
    summary.append(("OR-3 (p=1/2)", r["l2_defect"], r["poincare_defect"]))

    r = analyse_event("Tribes: (0 AND 1) OR (2 AND 3)", Rat(1, 2), 4,
                      tribes([[0, 1], [2, 3]]))
    summary.append(("Tribes 2x2 (p=1/2)", r["l2_defect"], r["poincare_defect"]))

    r = analyse_event("2x2 grid: some row entirely open", Rat(1, 2), 4,
                      grid_row_crossing(2))
    summary.append(("2x2 crossing (p=1/2)", r["l2_defect"], r["poincare_defect"]))

    r = analyse_event("Majority of 5", Rat(1, 2), 5, majority(5))
    summary.append(("Majority-5 (p=1/2)", r["l2_defect"], r["poincare_defect"]))

    # ---- Part 4: the density sweep ---------------------------------------- #
    print("\n[4] Density sweep: how the two defects move with p (Majority of 3)")
    print(f"    {'p':>7} {'P':>12} {'P(1-P)':>14} {'l^2 defect':>14} "
          f"{'Poincare defect':>18}")
    for num in range(1, 10):
        p = Rat(num, 10)
        member = majority(3)
        g = sign_indicator(3, member)
        ghat = fourier_coefficients(p, 3, g)
        en = level_energies(p, 3, ghat)
        P = probability(p, 3, member)
        l2d = sum(en[s] for s in range(8) if popcount(s) >= 2) / 4
        pod = sum((Rat(popcount(s)) - 1) * en[s] for s in range(1, 8)) / 4
        print(f"    {str(p):>7} {str(P):>12} {str(P * (1 - P)):>14} "
              f"{str(l2d):>14} {str(pod):>18}")

    # ---- Part 5: summary --------------------------------------------------- #
    print("\n[5] Summary of exact defects")
    print(f"    {'event':<28} {'l^2 defect':>16} {'Poincare defect':>18} "
          f"{'ratio':>10}")
    for name, l2d, pod in summary:
        ratio = "inf" if l2d == 0 and pod > 0 else (
            "0/0" if l2d == 0 else str(pod / l2d))
        print(f"    {name:<28} {str(l2d):>16} {str(pod):>18} {ratio:>10}")
    print("\n    Note: the Poincare defect always dominates the l^2 defect,")
    print("    since 1[|S| >= 2] <= |S| - 1 for every nonempty S; they coincide")
    print("    exactly when all high-degree energy sits at degree 2.")

    print("\n" + "=" * 78)
    print("  All identities verified exactly in rational arithmetic.")
    print("=" * 78)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

demos.name: Exhaustive Enumeration of Monotone Events and the Extremal Classification of Both Influence Inequalities
demos.description: Enumerates every upward-closed (monotone) event on N = 1, 2, 3 and 4 sites -- the Dedekind counts 3, 6, 20 and 168 -- and, for each one at several rational densities, tests the three-way equivalence between tightness of the l-squared influence bound, tightness of the variance-influence Poincare inequality, and vanishing of all Fourier coefficients of degree at least two. Every case is checked exactly, and the script reports the complete list of extremal events: on each site set they are precisely the two constants and the N dictatorships, so every genuinely multi-site monotone event has a strictly positive gap in both inequalities simultaneously. A second pass maximises the level-at-least-two spectral energy over all monotone events, locating the event furthest from extremality on each cube.
demos.code:
"""
Exhaustive search over every monotone event on a small site set, testing the
unified equality criterion.

Theory says that for an increasing event A on N sites with 0 < p < 1, writing
P = P_p(A), pq = p(1-p), I_v for the influences and E_S for the level energies
of the +/-1 indicator:

    (a)  pq sum_v I_v^2  =  P(1-P)          (the l^2 bound is tight)
    (b)  P(1-P)          =  pq sum_v I_v    (Poincare is tight)
    (c)  ghat(S) = 0 for every |S| >= 2     (the event has Fourier degree <= 1)

are *equivalent*.  This script enumerates all monotone events on N = 1, 2, 3, 4
sites -- the Dedekind numbers 3, 6, 20, 168 of upward-closed families,
including the two trivial ones -- and checks the equivalence exactly, at several
rational densities.  It then reports exactly which events achieve equality.

The prediction is that only the trivial events (always / never) and the
dictatorships have degree <= 1, so those are the only extremal cases; and the
script confirms it by exhibiting the full list.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple

Rat = Fraction


def popcount(x: int) -> int:
    return bin(x).count("1")


def biased_transform(f: List[Rat], n: int, p: Rat) -> List[Rat]:
    """Division-free O(n 2^n) biased Fourier transform."""
    q = 1 - p
    F = list(f)
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for eta in range(1 << n):
            if eta & bit:
                continue
            a, b = F[eta], F[eta | bit]
            F[eta] = p * b + q * a
            F[eta | bit] = b - a
    return F


def weight(p: Rat, n: int, eta: int) -> Rat:
    q = 1 - p
    w = Rat(1)
    for v in range(n):
        w *= p if (eta >> v) & 1 else q
    return w


def monotone_events(n: int) -> List[Tuple[bool, ...]]:
    """All upward-closed subsets of the n-cube, as membership tuples."""
    out = []
    for bits in product([False, True], repeat=1 << n):
        ok = True
        for e in range(1 << n):
            if bits[e]:
                for v in range(n):
                    if not bits[e | (1 << v)]:
                        ok = False
                        break
            if not ok:
                break
        if ok:
            out.append(bits)
    return out


def describe(bits: Tuple[bool, ...], n: int) -> str:
    """A short human description of a monotone event."""
    if not any(bits):
        return "never"
    if all(bits):
        return "always"
    for v in range(n):
        if all(bits[e] == bool((e >> v) & 1) for e in range(1 << n)):
            return f"dictator on site {v}"
    minimal = []
    for e in range(1 << n):
        if bits[e] and all(not bits[e & ~(1 << v)] for v in range(n) if (e >> v) & 1):
            minimal.append("&".join(str(v) for v in range(n) if (e >> v) & 1) or "()")
    return " | ".join("(" + m + ")" for m in sorted(minimal, key=len))


def report(n: int, p: Rat) -> None:
    pq = p * (1 - p)
    events = monotone_events(n)
    extremal: List[str] = []
    for bits in events:
        g = [Rat(1) if bits[e] else Rat(-1) for e in range(1 << n)]
        ghat = biased_transform(g, n, p)
        prob = sum(weight(p, n, e) for e in range(1 << n) if bits[e])
        infl = [sum(weight(p, n, e) for e in range(1 << n)
                    if bits[e | (1 << v)] and not bits[e & ~(1 << v)])
                for v in range(n)]

        a = (pq * sum(i * i for i in infl) == prob * (1 - prob))
        b = (prob * (1 - prob) == pq * sum(infl))
        c = all(ghat[s] == 0 for s in range(1 << n) if popcount(s) >= 2)
        assert a == b == c, f"equality criterion failed on {bits}"
        if c:
            extremal.append(describe(bits, n))

    print(f"  N = {n}, p = {p}: {len(events):>4} monotone events, "
          f"{len(extremal)} extremal")
    print(f"      extremal events: {', '.join(extremal)}")


def spectral_concentration(n: int, p: Rat) -> None:
    """
    How much of the spectral mass of a monotone event can sit above degree one?
    The answer bounds both defects; here we simply maximise it by brute force.
    """
    pq = p * (1 - p)
    best: Tuple[Rat, str] = (Rat(0), "")
    for bits in monotone_events(n):
        g = [Rat(1) if bits[e] else Rat(-1) for e in range(1 << n)]
        ghat = biased_transform(g, n, p)
        high = sum(pq ** popcount(s) * ghat[s] ** 2
                   for s in range(1 << n) if popcount(s) >= 2)
        if high > best[0]:
            best = (high, describe(bits, n))
    print(f"  N = {n}, p = {p}: largest level-(>=2) energy is {best[0]} "
          f"(= {float(best[0]):.4f}), attained by  {best[1]}")
    print(f"      this is 4x the largest possible l^2 defect at this density")


def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("  EXHAUSTIVE TEST OF THE UNIFIED EQUALITY CRITERION")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("\n[A] every monotone event, every criterion, exact arithmetic")
    for n in (1, 2, 3, 4):
        for p in (Rat(1, 2), Rat(1, 3)):
            report(n, p)

    print("\n[B] how far from extremal can a monotone event be?")
    for n in (2, 3, 4):
        spectral_concentration(n, Rat(1, 2))

    print("\n  Conclusion: on every site set tested, the only monotone events with")
    print("  Fourier degree <= 1 -- equivalently, the only events for which either")
    print("  influence inequality is an equality -- are the two constants and the")
    print("  dictatorships.  Every other monotone event has a strictly positive")
    print("  gap in BOTH inequalities simultaneously.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

algorithms.name: Division-Free Biased Fast Fourier Transform on the Discrete Cube
algorithms.description: Computes all 2^N p-biased Fourier coefficients of a function on the N-site cube in O(N 2^N) arithmetic operations, using no divisions whatsoever. The mathematical foundation is the exact one-coordinate decomposition f = A_v f + psi_v D_v f, in which the v-average A_v f and the v-derivative D_v f both ignore the coordinate v, together with the identity that the coefficient of f at a frequency S containing v equals the coefficient of D_v f at S minus v, while the coefficient at a frequency omitting v equals that of A_v f. Processing one coordinate at a time therefore splits the frequency space into the halves 'contains v' and 'omits v', exactly as in a radix-2 butterfly. The normalizing powers (p(1-p))^{|S|} that appear in the definition of the coefficient are cancelled precisely by the recursion, which is why the algorithm is division-free -- a property that makes it exact over the rationals and numerically benign near p = 0 and p = 1. The inverse transform runs the same butterfly backwards, each step solving a 2x2 system of determinant 1. Naive evaluation from the definition costs O(N 4^N) by comparison.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT : f, a table of 2^N reals indexed by configurations of N sites
        p, a density with 0 < p < 1;   set q <- 1 - p
OUTPUT: F, a table of 2^N reals with F[S] = fhat(S), S read as a bitmask

1  F <- copy of f
2  for v <- 0 to N-1 do
3      bit <- 2^v
4      for each configuration eta with bit v equal to 0 do
5          a <- F[eta]                # value with site v closed
6          b <- F[eta OR bit]         # value with site v open
7          F[eta]       <- p*b + q*a  # v-average:    frequency omits v
8          F[eta OR bit] <- b - a     # v-derivative: frequency has v
9      end for
10 end for
11 return F

INVARIANT after processing coordinates 0..v:
   for every frequency S contained in {0..v}, the entry indexed by the
   bitmask of S holds fhat(S) exactly.

COMPLEXITY: N * 2^(N-1) butterflies, i.e. O(N 2^N) time, O(2^N) space,
            zero divisions; exact when p is rational.

INVERSE (same loop reversed):
   avg <- F[eta];  der <- F[eta OR bit]
   F[eta] <- avg - p*der ;  F[eta OR bit] <- avg + q*der
algorithms.code:
"""
Division-free biased fast Fourier transform on the discrete cube.

For a finite site set of size N, a density p in (0,1) and q = 1 - p, the
p-biased Walsh characters are

    psi_v(eta) = eta_v - p,        psi_S = prod_{v in S} psi_v,

and the Fourier coefficients of f : {0,1}^N -> R are

    fhat(S) = E_p[f psi_S] / (p q)^{|S|}.

Evaluating this definition directly costs O(N 4^N).  The transform below costs
O(N 2^N) and, remarkably, performs no division whatsoever.

The mechanism is the exact one-coordinate splitting

    f = A_v f + psi_v * D_v f,
    A_v f (eta) = p f(eta with v open) + q f(eta with v closed),
    D_v f (eta) = f(eta with v open) - f(eta with v closed),

in which both pieces are independent of the coordinate v, combined with the
identity  fhat(S) = (D_v f)^(S \\ v)  valid for every S containing v, and
fhat(S) = (A_v f)^(S) for every S omitting v.  Processing one coordinate at a
time therefore separates the frequency space into the halves "S contains v" and
"S omits v", and the normalising powers (p q)^{|S|} are cancelled exactly by the
recursion -- which is why no division appears.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence, Union

Num = Union[Fraction, float]


def biased_fast_transform(f: Sequence[Num], n: int, p: Num) -> List[Num]:
    """
    Return the array `F` of p-biased Fourier coefficients of `f`.

    Parameters
    ----------
    f : table of 2^n values, indexed by configuration (bit v set = site v open)
    n : number of sites
    p : density, 0 < p < 1 (a Fraction gives an exact result)

    Returns
    -------
    F : table of 2^n values; F[S], with S read as the bitmask of a set of sites,
        equals fhat(S).

    Complexity
    ----------
    Time O(n 2^n), space O(2^n), zero divisions.
    """
    q = 1 - p
    F: List[Num] = list(f)
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for eta in range(1 << n):
            if eta & bit:
                continue
            a = F[eta]            # site v closed
            b = F[eta | bit]      # site v open
            F[eta] = p * b + q * a        # v-average  -> frequencies omitting v
            F[eta | bit] = b - a          # v-derivative -> frequencies containing v
    return F


def inverse_biased_transform(fhat: Sequence[Num], n: int, p: Num) -> List[Num]:
    """
    Invert the transform: reconstruct f from its coefficients via
    f = sum_S fhat(S) psi_S.  Runs the butterfly backwards in O(n 2^n).
    """
    q = 1 - p
    F: List[Num] = list(fhat)
    for v in reversed(range(n)):
        bit = 1 << v
        for eta in range(1 << n):
            if eta & bit:
                continue
            avg = F[eta]          # p*b + q*a
            der = F[eta | bit]    # b - a
            a = avg - p * der     # solve the 2x2 system (determinant 1)
            b = avg + q * der
            F[eta] = a
            F[eta | bit] = b
    return F


def level_energies(fhat: Sequence[Num], n: int, p: Num) -> List[Num]:
    """E_S(f) = (p q)^{|S|} fhat(S)^2 for each frequency S."""
    pq = p * (1 - p)
    return [pq ** bin(s).count("1") * fhat[s] ** 2 for s in range(1 << n)]


def weight(p: Num, n: int, eta: int) -> Num:
    """Probability of a single configuration under the p-biased product measure."""
    q = 1 - p
    w: Num = 1
    for v in range(n):
        w = w * (p if (eta >> v) & 1 else q)
    return w


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Exact round trip and exact Parseval check on a random rational function.
    import random

    rng = random.Random(7)
    n, p = 4, Fraction(2, 5)
    f = [Fraction(rng.randint(-9, 9), rng.randint(1, 6)) for _ in range(1 << n)]

    fhat = biased_fast_transform(f, n, p)
    back = inverse_biased_transform(fhat, n, p)
    print("round trip exact :", back == f)

    lhs = sum(weight(p, n, e) * f[e] * f[e] for e in range(1 << n))
    rhs = sum(level_energies(fhat, n, p))
    print("Parseval exact   :", lhs == rhs, " E[f^2] =", lhs)

algorithms.name: Exact Level-Energy Ledger and Simultaneous Defect Analysis for Monotone Events
algorithms.description: Given a monotone event on N sites and a rational density p, this procedure computes the complete spectral ledger of the event and, from it, both influence inequalities together with their exact defects. It first forms the plus-or-minus-one indicator, applies the division-free biased transform to obtain all coefficients, and squares them against the weights (p(1-p))^{|S|} to produce the level energies E_S, which are nonnegative and provably sum to exactly one. It then computes the probability P of the event and the influence of each site by direct enumeration of pivotal configurations. The two defects are read off the same ledger under different weightings: the l-squared defect is a quarter of the energy at all levels of degree at least two, and the Poincare defect is a quarter of the energy of each nonempty level counted with multiplicity one less than its cardinality. Because both quantities are also computable directly from P and the influences, the routine asserts every identity of the theory as it goes -- Plancherel, Margulis-Russo, the energy decomposition, the Poincare defect identity, and the equivalence between vanishing defects and Fourier degree at most one -- so a run is itself a proof-checking pass on a finite instance. Total cost O(N 2^N) in exact rational arithmetic.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT : N, a rational density p in (0,1), a predicate member(eta)
        describing an upward-closed event
OUTPUT: the level energies, the influences, and both exact defects

 1  assert monotonicity: for every eta with member(eta) and every site v,
       member(eta with v opened) must hold
 2  q <- 1 - p ;  pq <- p*q
 3  g[eta] <- +1 if member(eta) else -1,  for all 2^N configurations
 4  ghat <- BiasedFFT(g, p)                        # O(N 2^N)
 5  E[S]  <- pq^popcount(S) * ghat[S]^2            # the ledger
 6  P     <- sum of w_p(eta) over eta with member(eta)
 7  for each site v:
 8      I[v] <- sum of w_p(eta) over eta such that
                member(eta with v opened) and not member(eta with v closed)
 9  l2_lhs  <- pq * sum_v I[v]^2
10  mid     <- P*(1-P)
11  poin_rhs<- pq * sum_v I[v]
12  l2_defect   <- (1/4) * sum over S with popcount(S) >= 2 of E[S]
13  poin_defect <- (1/4) * sum over nonempty S of (popcount(S)-1)*E[S]

14  ASSERT sum_S E[S] = 1                          # Plancherel
15  ASSERT ghat[{v}] = 2*I[v] for every site v     # Margulis-Russo
16  ASSERT mid = l2_lhs + l2_defect                # energy decomposition
17  ASSERT poin_rhs = mid + poin_defect            # Poincare defect
18  ASSERT (l2_defect = 0) <=> (poin_defect = 0)
               <=> (ghat[S] = 0 for all popcount(S) >= 2)
19  return E, I, l2_defect, poin_defect

COMPLEXITY: O(N 2^N) exact rational operations.
algorithms.code:
"""
Exact defect analysis for the two influence inequalities on the biased cube.

Given a monotone (increasing) event A on N sites and a rational density p, this
module computes, in exact rational arithmetic:

    P        = P_p(A)
    I_v      = P_p(site v is pivotal)                     (the influences)
    E_S      = (pq)^{|S|} ghat(S)^2                       (the level energies of
               the +/-1 indicator g of A; these sum to 1)

and then the two defects, which are two differently weighted readings of the
same ledger (E_S)_S:

    l^2 defect       = P(1-P) - pq sum_v I_v^2      = (1/4) sum_{|S| >= 2} E_S
    Poincare defect  = pq sum_v I_v - P(1-P)        = (1/4) sum_{S != 0} (|S|-1) E_S

Both are nonnegative; both vanish exactly when the event has Fourier degree at
most one.  Since 1[|S| >= 2] <= |S| - 1 for every nonempty S, the Poincare
defect always dominates the l^2 defect.

Complexity: O(N 2^N) for the spectrum (division-free butterfly) plus O(N 2^N)
for the influences, hence O(N 2^N) overall, with exact rational arithmetic.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Callable, Dict, List

Rat = Fraction


def popcount(x: int) -> int:
    return bin(x).count("1")


def biased_fast_transform(f: List[Rat], n: int, p: Rat) -> List[Rat]:
    """Division-free O(n 2^n) biased Fourier transform (see the companion routine)."""
    q = 1 - p
    F = list(f)
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for eta in range(1 << n):
            if eta & bit:
                continue
            a, b = F[eta], F[eta | bit]
            F[eta] = p * b + q * a
            F[eta | bit] = b - a
    return F


def weight(p: Rat, n: int, eta: int) -> Rat:
    q = 1 - p
    w = Rat(1)
    for v in range(n):
        w *= p if (eta >> v) & 1 else q
    return w


@dataclass
class DefectReport:
    """Everything the ledger says about one monotone event at one density."""
    n: int
    p: Rat
    prob: Rat
    influences: List[Rat]
    energies: List[Rat]
    total_energy: Rat
    l2_lhs: Rat                 # pq sum_v I_v^2
    l2_rhs: Rat                 # P(1-P)
    l2_defect: Rat
    poincare_lhs: Rat           # P(1-P)
    poincare_rhs: Rat           # pq sum_v I_v
    poincare_defect: Rat
    degree_le_one: bool
    profile: Dict[int, Rat] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def summary(self) -> str:
        lines = [
            f"N = {self.n}, p = {self.p}",
            f"  P                 = {self.prob}",
            f"  influences        = {[str(i) for i in self.influences]}",
            f"  total energy      = {self.total_energy}   (must be 1)",
            "  spectral profile  = "
            + ", ".join(f"deg {k}: {v}" for k, v in sorted(self.profile.items())),
            f"  l2       : {self.l2_lhs} <= {self.l2_rhs}   defect {self.l2_defect}",
            f"  Poincare : {self.poincare_lhs} <= {self.poincare_rhs}"
            f"   defect {self.poincare_defect}",
            f"  degree <= 1       = {self.degree_le_one}"
            f"  -> both bounds {'tight' if self.degree_le_one else 'strict'}",
        ]
        return "\n".join(lines)


def analyse(n: int, p: Rat, member: Callable[[int], bool]) -> DefectReport:
    """
    Full exact analysis.  `member(eta)` must describe an increasing event:
    if it holds for eta it must hold for every eta with more open sites.
    """
    for eta in range(1 << n):
        if member(eta):
            for v in range(n):
                assert member(eta | (1 << v)), "event is not increasing"

    q = 1 - p
    pq = p * q

    g = [Rat(1) if member(e) else Rat(-1) for e in range(1 << n)]
    ghat = biased_fast_transform(g, n, p)
    energies = [pq ** popcount(s) * ghat[s] ** 2 for s in range(1 << n)]

    prob = sum(weight(p, n, e) for e in range(1 << n) if member(e))

    influences: List[Rat] = []
    for v in range(n):
        tot = Rat(0)
        for eta in range(1 << n):
            if member(eta | (1 << v)) and not member(eta & ~(1 << v)):
                tot += weight(p, n, eta)
        influences.append(tot)

    var4 = 4 * prob * (1 - prob)
    l2_lhs = pq * sum(i * i for i in influences)
    l2_rhs = prob * (1 - prob)
    l2_defect = sum(energies[s] for s in range(1 << n) if popcount(s) >= 2) / 4

    poincare_rhs = pq * sum(influences)
    poincare_defect = sum((Rat(popcount(s)) - 1) * energies[s]
                          for s in range(1 << n) if s != 0) / 4

    # exact consistency assertions -- these ARE the theorems
    assert sum(energies) == 1, "Plancherel failed"
    assert var4 == 4 * l2_lhs + 4 * l2_defect, "energy decomposition failed"
    assert 4 * poincare_rhs - var4 == 4 * poincare_defect, "Poincare defect failed"
    for v in range(n):
        assert ghat[1 << v] == 2 * influences[v], "Margulis-Russo failed"

    degree_le_one = all(ghat[s] == 0 for s in range(1 << n) if popcount(s) >= 2)
    assert (l2_defect == 0) == degree_le_one
    assert (poincare_defect == 0) == degree_le_one

    profile: Dict[int, Rat] = {}
    for s in range(1 << n):
        profile[popcount(s)] = profile.get(popcount(s), Rat(0)) + energies[s]

    return DefectReport(
        n=n, p=p, prob=prob, influences=influences, energies=energies,
        total_energy=sum(energies),
        l2_lhs=l2_lhs, l2_rhs=l2_rhs, l2_defect=l2_defect,
        poincare_lhs=l2_rhs, poincare_rhs=poincare_rhs,
        poincare_defect=poincare_defect,
        degree_le_one=degree_le_one, profile=profile,
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    events = {
        "dictator on site 0": (3, lambda e: bool(e & 1)),
        "majority of 3":      (3, lambda e: popcount(e) >= 2),
        "AND of 3":           (3, lambda e: popcount(e) == 3),
        "tribes (0&1)|(2&3)": (4, lambda e: (e & 0b0011) == 0b0011
                               or (e & 0b1100) == 0b1100),
        "majority of 5":      (5, lambda e: popcount(e) >= 3),
    }
    for name, (n, member) in events.items():
        print(f"\n=== {name} ===")
        print(analyse(n, Fraction(1, 2), member).summary())

visualizations.name: Spectral Profiles by Degree and the Two Exact Influence Defects
visualizations.description: A two-panel figure at density one half. The left panel stacks, for six classic monotone events (dictator, AND, OR, majority of three, tribes, majority of five), the level energies of the plus-or-minus-one indicator aggregated by degree; every column sums to exactly one, which is the biased Plancherel identity made visible. The right panel puts the two exact defects side by side for the same events: the l-squared defect, which is a quarter of the energy above degree one, and the Poincare defect, which is a quarter of the same energies reweighted by cardinality minus one. The dictator column shows both defects collapsing to zero simultaneously -- the unified equality case -- while every other event shows the Poincare defect dominating the l-squared one, as the pointwise weight comparison predicts.
visualizations.code:
"""
Visualization: spectral profiles by degree, and the two influence defects.

Left panel  -- for a family of monotone events, the level energies
                   E_S = (pq)^{|S|} ghat(S)^2
               of the +/-1 indicator, aggregated by degree |S|.  These are
               nonnegative and sum to exactly 1 (the biased Plancherel identity
               for Boolean functions), so each column is a probability
               distribution over frequencies: the "spectral profile".

Right panel -- the exact defects of the two classical influence inequalities,
                   l^2 defect      = P(1-P) - pq sum_v I_v^2
                                   = (1/4) sum_{|S| >= 2} E_S
                   Poincare defect = pq sum_v I_v - P(1-P)
                                   = (1/4) sum_{S != 0} (|S| - 1) E_S
               Both vanish precisely for events of Fourier degree at most one
               (the dictatorship), and the Poincare defect always dominates.

Run:  python viz1_spectral_profiles.py       (writes spectral_profiles.png)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

Rat = Fraction


def popcount(x: int) -> int:
    return bin(x).count("1")


def biased_transform(f: List[Rat], n: int, p: Rat) -> List[Rat]:
    q = 1 - p
    F = list(f)
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for eta in range(1 << n):
            if eta & bit:
                continue
            a, b = F[eta], F[eta | bit]
            F[eta] = p * b + q * a
            F[eta | bit] = b - a
    return F


def weight(p: Rat, n: int, eta: int) -> Rat:
    q = 1 - p
    w = Rat(1)
    for v in range(n):
        w *= p if (eta >> v) & 1 else q
    return w


def analyse(n: int, p: Rat, member: Callable[[int], bool]
            ) -> Tuple[Dict[int, float], float, float]:
    pq = p * (1 - p)
    g = [Rat(1) if member(e) else Rat(-1) for e in range(1 << n)]
    ghat = biased_transform(g, n, p)
    en = [pq ** popcount(s) * ghat[s] ** 2 for s in range(1 << n)]

    prob = sum(weight(p, n, e) for e in range(1 << n) if member(e))
    infl = []
    for v in range(n):
        infl.append(sum(weight(p, n, e) for e in range(1 << n)
                        if member(e | (1 << v)) and not member(e & ~(1 << v))))

    profile: Dict[int, float] = {}
    for s in range(1 << n):
        profile[popcount(s)] = profile.get(popcount(s), 0.0) + float(en[s])

    l2_defect = float(sum(en[s] for s in range(1 << n) if popcount(s) >= 2)) / 4
    poin_defect = float(sum((Rat(popcount(s)) - 1) * en[s]
                            for s in range(1 << n) if s != 0)) / 4
    return profile, l2_defect, poin_defect


EVENTS: List[Tuple[str, int, Callable[[int], bool]]] = [
    ("Dictator\n(1 site)", 3, lambda e: bool(e & 1)),
    ("AND$_3$", 3, lambda e: popcount(e) == 3),
    ("OR$_3$", 3, lambda e: e != 0),
    ("Maj$_3$", 3, lambda e: popcount(e) >= 2),
    ("Tribes\n$(01)\\vee(23)$", 4, lambda e: (e & 3) == 3 or (e & 12) == 12),
    ("Maj$_5$", 5, lambda e: popcount(e) >= 3),
]


def main() -> None:
    p = Rat(1, 2)
    names, profiles, l2s, pois = [], [], [], []
    for name, n, member in EVENTS:
        prof, l2d, pod = analyse(n, p, member)
        names.append(name)
        profiles.append(prof)
        l2s.append(l2d)
        pois.append(pod)

    max_deg = max(max(prof) for prof in profiles)
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5.4))

    x = np.arange(len(names))
    bottoms = np.zeros(len(names))
    cmap = plt.get_cmap("viridis")
    for d in range(max_deg + 1):
        vals = np.array([prof.get(d, 0.0) for prof in profiles])
        ax1.bar(x, vals, bottom=bottoms, width=0.62,
                color=cmap(d / max(max_deg, 1)),
                edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.7,
                label=f"degree {d}")
        for xi, (v, b) in enumerate(zip(vals, bottoms)):
            if v > 0.045:
                ax1.text(xi, b + v / 2, f"{v:.3f}", ha="center", va="center",
                         fontsize=8, color="white", weight="bold")
        bottoms += vals

    ax1.set_xticks(x)
    ax1.set_xticklabels(names, fontsize=9)
    ax1.set_ylim(0, 1.32)
    ax1.set_ylabel("level energy  $E_S=(pq)^{|S|}\\hat g(S)^2$")
    ax1.set_title("Spectral profile by degree at $p=1/2$\n"
                  "(each column sums to exactly $1$: biased Plancherel)",
                  fontsize=11)
    ax1.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=3, loc="upper center", framealpha=0.9)
    ax1.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)

    w = 0.36
    ax2.bar(x - w / 2, l2s, width=w, color="#3b7dd8", edgecolor="white",
            label=r"$\ell^2$ defect $=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{|S|\geq 2}E_S$")
    ax2.bar(x + w / 2, pois, width=w, color="#d1495b", edgecolor="white",
            label=r"Poincare defect $=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{S\neq\emptyset}(|S|-1)E_S$")
    top = max(max(l2s), max(pois))
    for xi, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(l2s, pois)):
        ax2.text(xi - w / 2, a + 0.006 * top, f"{a:.4f}", ha="center", fontsize=7.5)
        ax2.text(xi + w / 2, b + 0.006 * top, f"{b:.4f}", ha="center", fontsize=7.5)
    ax2.set_ylim(0, top * 1.22)
    ax2.set_xticks(x)
    ax2.set_xticklabels(names, fontsize=9)
    ax2.set_ylabel("defect")
    ax2.set_title("The two influence defects, exactly\n"
                  "both vanish iff the event has degree $\\leq 1$", fontsize=11)
    ax2.legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="upper left", framealpha=0.9)
    ax2.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.25)

    fig.suptitle("One ledger, two readings: the level energies of a monotone event",
                 fontsize=13, weight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.94))
    fig.savefig("spectral_profiles.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote spectral_profiles.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

visualizations.description: For each of three monotone events (a dictator, majority of five, and a tribes function) the top row plots, as functions of the density p, the three curves of the influence sandwich: the lower bound p(1-p) times the sum of squared influences, the middle quantity P(1-P), and the upper bound p(1-p) times the total influence. The two gaps are shaded, and each shaded area is exactly the corresponding Fourier defect. The bottom row shows what drives them: the spectral mass of the event decomposed by degree as a stacked area over the same density range, totalling one at every p. For the dictator the three curves coincide identically -- all mass sits at degrees zero and one -- whereas for majority and tribes the high-degree bands swell near the threshold and the gaps open in step with them.
visualizations.code:
"""
Visualization: the influence sandwich and its two exact defects as the density
varies.

For a monotone event A on N sites, write P = P_p(A), q = 1 - p and let I_v be
the influence of site v.  The two classical influence inequalities sandwich the
variance-like quantity P(1-P):

        pq sum_v I_v^2   <=   P(1-P)   <=   pq sum_v I_v .

The complete p-biased Fourier expansion turns both inequalities into identities:
with the level energies E_S = (pq)^{|S|} ghat(S)^2 of the +/-1 indicator,

        P(1-P) - pq sum_v I_v^2 = (1/4) sum_{|S| >= 2} E_S          (lower gap)
        pq sum_v I_v - P(1-P)   = (1/4) sum_{S != 0} (|S|-1) E_S    (upper gap)

The top row plots the three curves with the two gaps shaded; the bottom row
plots the spectral profile by degree as a function of p, which is what actually
drives the gaps.

Run:  python viz2_density_sweep.py     (writes density_sweep.png)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def popcount(x: int) -> int:
    return bin(x).count("1")


def biased_transform(f: List[float], n: int, p: float) -> List[float]:
    """Division-free O(n 2^n) biased Fourier transform."""
    q = 1.0 - p
    F = list(f)
    for v in range(n):
        bit = 1 << v
        for eta in range(1 << n):
            if eta & bit:
                continue
            a, b = F[eta], F[eta | bit]
            F[eta] = p * b + q * a
            F[eta | bit] = b - a
    return F


def weight(p: float, n: int, eta: int) -> float:
    q = 1.0 - p
    w = 1.0
    for v in range(n):
        w *= p if (eta >> v) & 1 else q
    return w


def analyse(n: int, p: float, member: Callable[[int], bool]):
    pq = p * (1.0 - p)
    g = [1.0 if member(e) else -1.0 for e in range(1 << n)]
    ghat = biased_transform(g, n, p)
    en = [pq ** popcount(s) * ghat[s] ** 2 for s in range(1 << n)]

    prob = sum(weight(p, n, e) for e in range(1 << n) if member(e))
    infl = [sum(weight(p, n, e) for e in range(1 << n)
                if member(e | (1 << v)) and not member(e & ~(1 << v)))
            for v in range(n)]

    lo = pq * sum(i * i for i in infl)
    mid = prob * (1.0 - prob)
    hi = pq * sum(infl)

    profile: Dict[int, float] = {}
    for s in range(1 << n):
        profile[popcount(s)] = profile.get(popcount(s), 0.0) + en[s]
    return prob, lo, mid, hi, profile


EVENTS: List[Tuple[str, int, Callable[[int], bool]]] = [
    ("Dictator on one site  (degree 1: both bounds are equalities)",
     3, lambda e: bool(e & 1)),
    ("Majority of 5", 5, lambda e: popcount(e) >= 3),
    ("Tribes  $(x_0\\wedge x_1)\\vee(x_2\\wedge x_3)$", 4,
     lambda e: (e & 3) == 3 or (e & 12) == 12),
]


def main() -> None:
    ps = np.linspace(0.02, 0.98, 193)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, len(EVENTS), figsize=(15.5, 8.4),
                             gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.35, 1.0]})

    for col, (name, n, member) in enumerate(EVENTS):
        lo, mid, hi, probs = [], [], [], []
        prof_by_deg = {d: [] for d in range(n + 1)}
        for p in ps:
            prob, a, b, c, profile = analyse(n, float(p), member)
            probs.append(prob)
            lo.append(a)
            mid.append(b)
            hi.append(c)
            for d in range(n + 1):
                prof_by_deg[d].append(profile.get(d, 0.0))

        ax = axes[0][col]
        ax.fill_between(ps, lo, mid, color="#3b7dd8", alpha=0.28,
                        label=r"$\ell^2$ gap $=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{|S|\geq 2}E_S$")
        ax.fill_between(ps, mid, hi, color="#d1495b", alpha=0.25,
                        label=r"Poincare gap $=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{S\neq\emptyset}(|S|-1)E_S$")
        ax.plot(ps, lo, color="#3b7dd8", lw=2, label=r"$pq\sum_v I_v^2$")
        ax.plot(ps, mid, color="black", lw=2.2, label=r"$P(1-P)$")
        ax.plot(ps, hi, color="#d1495b", lw=2, label=r"$pq\sum_v I_v$")
        ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10.5)
        ax.set_xlabel("density $p$")
        ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
        ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
        if col == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel("value")
        ax.legend(fontsize=7.6, loc="upper right", framealpha=0.92)

        ax2 = axes[1][col]
        cmap = plt.get_cmap("viridis")
        bottoms = np.zeros(len(ps))
        for d in range(n + 1):
            vals = np.array(prof_by_deg[d])
            ax2.fill_between(ps, bottoms, bottoms + vals,
                             color=cmap(d / max(n, 1)),
                             label=f"deg {d}", linewidth=0)
            bottoms = bottoms + vals
        ax2.set_ylim(0, 1)
        ax2.set_xlim(0, 1)
        ax2.set_xlabel("density $p$")
        if col == 0:
            ax2.set_ylabel("spectral mass by degree\n(total $=1$)")
        ax2.legend(fontsize=7, ncol=3, loc="lower center", framealpha=0.85)

    fig.suptitle("The influence sandwich and its two exact Fourier defects",
                 fontsize=14, weight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.95))
    fig.savefig("density_sweep.png", dpi=155)
    print("wrote density_sweep.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

interactive_demos.title: The Spectral Ledger: Build a Monotone Event and Watch Both Inequalities Emerge
interactive_demos.description: A fully self-contained interactive laboratory for the p-biased Fourier expansion on a cube of four sites. The reader designs an event by toggling any of the sixteen configurations -- arranged by the number of open sites, so upward closure is visible at a glance -- or loads one of eight presets (dictator, majority, AND, OR, tribes, a two-by-two grid crossing, a threshold-two event, and a two-site conjunction), with a one-click button that forces upward closure. A slider sets the density p. Three linked panels then update live: the full spectral ledger, showing the level energy of each of the sixteen frequencies coloured by degree and always summing to exactly one; the influence sandwich, drawing the three quantities p(1-p) times the sum of squared influences, P(1-P), and p(1-p) times the total influence as horizontal bars with the two gaps bracketed and labelled by their exact Fourier expressions; and the spectral mass aggregated by degree. A running panel of verification badges recomputes, at every interaction, the Plancherel identity, the Margulis-Russo relation between degree-one coefficients and influences, the exact energy decomposition, the exact Poincare defect identity, and the equivalence between vanishing defects and Fourier degree at most one. Layered explanations behind collapsible sections develop the product rule, orthogonality, the reproducing kernel and the one-coordinate calculus for readers who want the derivations. Selecting the dictator preset makes both gaps collapse to zero at once; any other genuinely multi-site event opens both at once.

The Spectral Ledger of a Monotone Event

Pick any upward-closed event on four sites, slide the density p, and watch the same list of nonnegative level energies produce both of the classical influence inequalities — and their exact gaps.

1 · Choose the event


Click a configuration to toggle whether the event holds there. A configuration is written as the four site states, site 0 leftmost; rows are grouped by the number of open sites.

2 · Choose the density

density p0.500
p(1−p)0.2500

3 · Read the numbers

P = probability of the event—
P(1−P)—
total energy ΣS ES—

The ledger: level energies ES = (pq)|S| Ŵ(S)²

Each bar is one frequency — one subset S of the four sites. The bars are nonnegative and always sum to exactly 1. Colour encodes the degree |S|. Degree 0 is the mean, degree 1 carries the influences, and everything above degree 1 is precisely what makes both classical inequalities strict.

The sandwich and its two exact gaps

Spectral mass by degree

What am I looking at? — the one-paragraph version

Four sites are independently open with probability p. An event is a rule saying, for each of the 16 configurations, whether it holds. The event is increasing if opening more sites never destroys it. Its influence at site v, written Iv, is the chance that site v is pivotal: the event holds when v is open and fails when v is closed. Two classical inequalities sandwich the quantity P(1−P): p(1−p) ΣIv² ≤ P(1−P) ≤ p(1−p) ΣIv. The panels above show that both gaps are read off one and the same list of numbers.

Click to reveal: the characters, the coefficients, and why the ledger exists

For each site v define the centred character ψv(η) = ηv − p, equal to 1−p when v is open and −p when it is closed. It has mean 0 and variance p(1−p). For a set S of sites put ψS = ∏v∈Sψv, with ψ∅ = 1.

The engine is the product rule: the expectation of a product of one-site functions factorises, E[∏v gv(ηv)] = ∏v(p gv(1) + (1−p) gv(0)). This is exactly independence, written so that algebra can use it. Applying it to ψSψT gives orthogonality: E[ψSψT] = (p(1−p))|S| if S = T, and 0 otherwise — a single mismatched site kills the whole product.

Hence the Fourier coefficient ƒ̂(S) = E[f ψS] / (p(1−p))|S| and the level energy ES = (p(1−p))|S| ƒ̂(S)² ≥ 0. Summing all 2N characters gives a reproducing kernel that is a Dirac delta reweighted by the measure, from which every function equals the sum of its Fourier series, and Parseval holds: E[fg] = ΣS(p(1−p))|S|ƒ̂(S)ĝ(S). For a ±1-valued indicator this forces ΣSES = 1 — the total shown in the panel.

Click to reveal: why both inequalities come from this one list

Write g for the ±1 indicator of the event, P for its probability. Two calibration facts: the empty level carries E∅ = (2P−1)², and the degree-one coefficients are the influences, ĝ({v}) = 2 Iv, so E{v} = 4p(1−p) Iv². Splitting the identity ΣSES = 1 into degree 0, degree 1 and the rest gives the exact energy decomposition

4P(1−P) = 4p(1−p) ΣvIv² + Σ|S|≥2ES.

So the ℓ² influence bound is the statement that the last sum is nonnegative.

For the other side, split a function at one coordinate: f = Avf + ψv Dvf, where Dvf is the discrete derivative and both pieces ignore the coordinate v. Two one-site integrals then give the site-energy identity ΣS∋vES = p(1−p) E[(Dvf)²]. Summing over v counts each level S exactly |S| times, while the variance counts each nonempty level once; subtracting gives the exact Poincaré defect

4p(1−p) ΣvIv − 4P(1−P) = ΣS≠∅(|S|−1) ES.

Same ledger, different weights: 1[|S|≥2] versus |S|−1. Both vanish exactly when the event has no Fourier weight above degree one — try the Dictator preset and watch both gaps collapse to zero.

Further reading: analysis of Boolean functions · percolation theory · the Efron–Stein inequality · Poincaré inequalities

interactive_layout:
# One Ledger, Two Inequalities
### A guided tour of the $p$-biased Fourier expansion on the discrete cube

---

## 0. The question, in one picture

Imagine $N$ switches. Each is independently **open** with probability $p$ and **closed** with probability $1-p$. An **event** is a rule that looks at the whole configuration and answers *yes* or *no* — "is there an open path across the grid?", "did a majority vote yes?", "is switch 3 open?". The event is **increasing** if opening more switches never turns a *yes* into a *no*.

Two quantities govern everything:

- $P$, the probability that the event holds;
- $I_v$, the **influence** of switch $v$ — the probability that $v$ is *pivotal*, i.e. that the answer is *yes* when $v$ is open and *no* when it is closed.

For decades two inequalities have sandwiched the variance-like quantity $P(1-P)$ between two functions of the influences:

$$p(1-p)\sum_v I_v^2 \;\le\; P(1-P) \;\le\; p(1-p)\sum_v I_v .$$

The upper bound is a Poincaré inequality; the lower one gives the square-root law $\sum_v I_v \le \sqrt{N}$ at $p=1/2$. They were proved by completely different arguments and they point in opposite directions.

**This page shows that both gaps are the same object.** Play with the widget below first — then we will build the machinery that explains it.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

> **Try this before reading on.** Select the *Dictator* preset. Both coloured gap bars collapse to zero: the two inequalities become equalities *simultaneously*. Now select *Majority* or *Tribes* — both gaps open up at once. Then slide $p$ and watch the bottom panel: the spectral mass migrates between degrees, and the gaps follow it exactly.

---

## 1. The cube, the measure, and the expectation

A configuration $\eta$ assigns *open* or *closed* to each of the $N$ sites, so there are $2^N$ of them. Because the switches are independent, the probability of a specific configuration is a product:

$$w_p(\eta) \;=\; \prod_{v}\bigl(p \text{ if } v \text{ open},\ 1-p \text{ if } v \text{ closed}\bigr),$$

and the expectation of any function $f$ on configurations is $\mathbb{E}_p[f] = \sum_\eta w_p(\eta)f(\eta)$. Two functions $f,g$ have inner product $\langle f,g\rangle = \mathbb{E}_p[fg]$. That is all the structure we need — no measure theory, no limits, nothing infinite.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal: the one theorem that does all the work</summary>

**The product rule.** For any family of one-site functions $g_v : \{\text{open},\text{closed}\}\to\mathbb{R}$,

$$\mathbb{E}_p\Bigl[\prod_v g_v(\eta_v)\Bigr] \;=\; \prod_v\bigl(p\,g_v(\text{open}) + (1-p)\,g_v(\text{closed})\bigr).$$

*Proof.* Expand the right-hand side by the distributive law. A product of $N$ two-term sums is a sum of $2^N$ products, one for each way of choosing a term from each factor — that is, one for each configuration $\eta$. The chosen probability factors multiply to $w_p(\eta)$ and the chosen function values multiply to $\prod_v g_v(\eta_v)$. $\blacksquare$

This is *exactly* the statement that the coordinates are independent, written in a form ready for algebra. Everything below is an application of it.
</details>

---

## 2. Characters: the harmonics of a coin flip

For each site $v$, the simplest nonconstant function that looks only at $v$ is its recentred state,

$$\psi_v(\eta) \;=\; \eta_v - p \;=\; \begin{cases}1-p, & v \text{ open},\\ -p, & v \text{ closed},\end{cases}$$

which has mean $0$ and variance $p(1-p)$. For a *set* $S$ of sites, form the overtone

$$\psi_S \;=\; \prod_{v \in S}\psi_v, \qquad \psi_\emptyset \equiv 1 .$$

The set $S$ is the *frequency* and $|S|$ is the *degree*.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal: why these are orthogonal, in three lines</summary>

Write $\psi_S\psi_T$ as a product over **all** coordinates: the factor at $v$ is $\psi_v^2$ if $v\in S\cap T$, $\psi_v$ if $v$ lies in exactly one of them, and $1$ otherwise. Apply the product rule. The local expectations are $\mathbb{E}[\psi_v^2] = p(1-p)$, $\mathbb{E}[\psi_v] = 0$, and $1$ respectively. So

$$\mathbb{E}_p[\psi_S\psi_T] = \begin{cases}\bigl(p(1-p)\bigr)^{|S|}, & S = T,\\ 0, & S \neq T,\end{cases}$$

because a *single* site in the symmetric difference contributes a zero factor and annihilates the whole product.
</details>

Orthogonality lets us define the **Fourier coefficient** and the **level energy**

$$\hat f(S) = \frac{\mathbb{E}_p[f\,\psi_S]}{\bigl(p(1-p)\bigr)^{|S|}}, \qquad E_S(f) = \bigl(p(1-p)\bigr)^{|S|}\hat f(S)^2 \;\ge\; 0 .$$

The bar chart in the widget above is exactly the list $(E_S)_S$. **That list is the ledger.**

---

## 3. Nothing is left over: completeness

Orthogonality alone would only give an *inequality* (Bessel's), and that is precisely why the two classical influence bounds are inequalities: the family of low-degree characters is incomplete. Completeness is what upgrades them.

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal: the reproducing kernel, and the collapse of the double sum</summary>

Sum the normalized products of characters over **all** $2^N$ frequencies. A sum over subsets of a product is a product of binomials:

$$K(\xi,\eta) = \sum_S \prod_{v\in S}\frac{\psi_v(\xi)\psi_v(\eta)}{p(1-p)} = \prod_v\left(1 + \frac{\psi_v(\xi)\psi_v(\eta)}{p(1-p)}\right).$$

Inspect one factor:

- $\xi_v \ne \eta_v$: the numerator is $(1-p)(-p)$, the bracket is $-1+1 = 0$. **One disagreement kills everything.**
- $\xi_v = \eta_v = $ open: the bracket is $1 + (1-p)/p = 1/p$.
- $\xi_v = \eta_v = $ closed: the bracket is $1 + p/(1-p) = 1/(1-p)$.

So $K(\xi,\eta) = \mathbb{1}[\xi=\eta]/w_p(\eta)$ — a Dirac delta reweighted by exactly the measure. Plugging this into $\sum_S \hat f(S)\psi_S(\eta)$ and swapping the sums collapses everything to $f(\eta)$.

$$\boxed{\ f = \sum_S \hat f(S)\,\psi_S \quad\text{and}\quad \mathbb{E}_p[fg] = \sum_S \bigl(p(1-p)\bigr)^{|S|}\hat f(S)\hat g(S).\ }$$

Taking $g=f$ and peeling off $S=\emptyset$ gives $\operatorname{Var}_p(f) = \sum_{S\ne\emptyset}E_S(f)$: **variance is total nonconstant energy.**
</details>

For a $\pm1$-valued indicator $g$ of an event, $g^2 \equiv 1$, so Parseval forces

$$\sum_S E_S(g) \;=\; 1 .$$

The energies form a probability distribution over frequencies. That is the "total energy" reading in the widget, and it stays pinned at $1.000000$ no matter what you do.

---

## 4. Reading the two inequalities off the ledger

Two calibration facts turn the abstract ledger into influence statistics:

- $E_\emptyset = (2P-1)^2$;
- $\hat g(\{v\}) = 2I_v$, hence $E_{\{v\}} = 4p(1-p)I_v^2$. *(This is the Fourier form of the Margulis–Russo formula — check it in the widget's influence table, where the two columns always agree.)*

Split $\sum_S E_S = 1$ into degree $0$, degree $1$, and the rest:

$$4P(1-P) \;=\; 4p(1-p)\sum_v I_v^2 \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{|S|\ge2}E_S}_{\ge\,0} .$$

**The $\ell^2$ influence bound is nothing but the nonnegativity of the last sum.**

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal: the other inequality, from one-coordinate calculus</summary>

Split a function at a single coordinate:

$$f = A_vf + \psi_v\,D_vf, \qquad D_vf(\eta) = f(\eta^{v\to\text{open}}) - f(\eta^{v\to\text{closed}}),$$

with $A_vf$ the average over $v$'s state. Both pieces ignore the coordinate $v$. Two one-site integrals ($\mathbb{E}[\psi_v h] = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}[\psi_v^2 h] = p(1-p)\mathbb{E}[h]$ for $v$-independent $h$) then give $\hat f(S) = \widehat{D_vf}(S\setminus v)$ for $S \ni v$, hence the **site-energy identity**

$$\sum_{S\ni v}E_S(f) \;=\; p(1-p)\,\mathbb{E}_p\bigl[(D_vf)^2\bigr].$$

Summing over $v$ counts each level $|S|$ times; the variance counts each nonempty level once. Subtract:

$$p(1-p)\sum_v\mathbb{E}_p\bigl[(D_vf)^2\bigr] - \operatorname{Var}_p(f) \;=\; \sum_{S\ne\emptyset}\bigl(|S|-1\bigr)E_S(f) \;\ge\;0 .$$

That is the Poincaré (Efron–Stein) inequality **for every real function**, with an exact remainder. For an increasing event $D_vg \in \{0,2\}$, so $\mathbb{E}[(D_vg)^2] = 4I_v$, and the identity becomes

$$4p(1-p)\sum_v I_v - 4P(1-P) \;=\; \sum_{S\ne\emptyset}\bigl(|S|-1\bigr)E_S .$$
</details>

Side by side:

| Inequality | Exact defect |
|---|---|
| $p(1-p)\sum_v I_v^2 \le P(1-P)$ | $\tfrac14\sum_S \mathbb{1}[|S|\ge2]\,E_S$ |
| $P(1-P) \le p(1-p)\sum_v I_v$ | $\tfrac14\sum_{S\ne\emptyset}(|S|-1)\,E_S$ |

Same ledger, two weightings. Since $\mathbb{1}[k\ge2]\le k-1$ for every integer $k\ge1$, the Poincaré gap always dominates — and both vanish under **the identical condition**: no Fourier weight above degree one.

---

## 5. See it across a family of events

The picture below computes the ledger for six classic monotone events at $p=1/2$. Note how the dictatorship puts all its energy at degree $1$ (both gaps zero), while majority and tribes leak energy upward and open both gaps at once.

{{visualization:0}}

And here is what happens as the density sweeps from $0$ to $1$: the sandwich, the two shaded gaps, and underneath, the spectral mass migrating between degrees that drives them.

{{visualization:1}}

---

## 6. Computing the ledger fast

Naively, extracting all $2^N$ coefficients costs $O(N4^N)$. But the one-coordinate splitting $f = A_vf + \psi_v D_vf$ *is* a butterfly step: it separates the frequencies containing $v$ from those omitting it. Iterating over coordinates gives an $O(N2^N)$ transform — and, delightfully, one that needs **no division at all**, because the normalizing powers $(p(1-p))^{|S|}$ cancel exactly against the recursion.

{{algorithm:0}}

With the spectrum in hand, every quantity in this page is one pass over the frequencies.

{{algorithm:1}}

---

## 7. Verify everything, exactly

Rational arithmetic means these identities can be checked with *no* floating-point slack. The following program verifies orthogonality, completeness, Parseval, Plancherel, Margulis–Russo, the energy decomposition, the site-energy identity, the Efron–Stein defect and the equality criterion — on dictatorships, majorities, AND/OR, tribes, grid crossing, and randomly generated non-Boolean functions.

{{demo:0}}

Finally, an exhaustive sweep: enumerate *every* upward-closed event on up to four sites and test the unified equality criterion on each. The conclusion is striking — only the constants and the dictatorships are extremal, so every genuinely multi-site monotone event has a strictly positive gap in **both** inequalities at once.

{{demo:1}}

---

## 8. Where this is going

The whole development rests on the product rule, which is the statement that the measure is a product measure. That is also exactly the mechanism behind **tensorization**, and tensorization is how a two-point hypercontractive estimate becomes an $N$-point one. Hypercontractivity is the one missing ingredient between what is on this page and the modern theory of influences — the $\log N/N$ lower bound on the maximal influence, Talagrand's refinement, Friedgut's junta theorem, and the noise-sensitivity picture of percolation.

In other words: the ledger is complete. What remains is to learn how the mass distributes across its levels.

Further reading: [analysis of Boolean functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analysis_of_Boolean_functions) · [Efron–Stein inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efron%E2%80%93Stein_inequality) · [percolation theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percolation_theory) · [Walsh functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walsh_function)
